content: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) can cause both acute and chronic infections. Acute HCV infection is defined as the presence of the virus within six months of exposure and infection. This phase is often asymptomatic and rarely associated with life-threatening conditions. In 15–45% of cases, acute HCV infection resolves spontaneously within six months without treatment. However, the remaining 55–85% of individuals, if untreated, will develop chronic HCV infection, harboring the virus for life. During acute infection, anti-HCV antibodies are produced and persist throughout life. The risk of developing cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) varies depending on individual patient characteristics and behaviors. HCV-related disease is not limited to the liver; extrahepatic manifestations include cryoglobulinemia, glomerulonephritis, thyroiditis, Sjögren syndrome, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and skin disorders such as porphyria cutanea tarda and lichen planus. In high-income countries, liver disease associated with HCV has become a leading cause of death among people living with HIV in the era of combination antiretroviral therapy (ART), accounting for approximately 47% of deaths in one U.S. cohort. Studies in Europe have shown that HIV/HCV co-infected individuals experience impaired CD4 recovery after ART initiation compared to those with HIV alone. Co-infected individuals also demonstrate faster HIV disease progression and impaired CD4 cell recovery. Preventing HCV infection is challenging due to the diverse routes of transmission and affected populations. Globally, most HCV infections occur in healthcare settings due to inadequate infection control practices, such as the reuse of injection equipment or transfusion of unscreened blood. People who inject drugs (PWID) are at high risk of HCV infection through contaminated injection equipment and non-injection drug use. Interventions targeting PWID include needle and syringe programs, opioid substitution therapy, and education on safe practices. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends comprehensive measures to prevent HCV transmission, including hand hygiene, safe handling and disposal of sharps, proper cleaning of medical equipment, blood screening, and training of healthcare personnel. For PWID, specific interventions include rapid hepatitis B vaccination, sterile needle and syringe programs, peer interventions, and integration of opioid dependence treatment with hepatitis care. Sexual transmission of HCV is rare among heterosexual couples but higher among men who have sex with men (MSM), particularly those with HIV co-infection. Mother-to-child transmission of HCV remains difficult to prevent, as no proven interventions exist. Neither delivery method nor breastfeeding has been reliably linked to transmission. The development of safe and effective HCV drugs for use during pregnancy may offer future solutions. Screening for HCV infection involves serological testing, followed by nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA to confirm chronic infection. Co-infections with other bloodborne viruses, such as HBV and HIV, should also be screened. In certain high-risk groups, such as people living with HIV, prisoners, and PWID, screening for tuberculosis (TB) is also recommended. The clinical spectrum of HCV-related disease ranges from mild fibrosis to cirrhosis and HCC. Compensated cirrhosis may progress to decompensated cirrhosis, characterized by ascites, varices, liver failure, renal failure, and sepsis, all of which are life-threatening. HCC occurs at an annual rate of 2–4% in individuals with cirrhosis. Disease staging, through liver biopsy or non-invasive methods, is critical for identifying patients with advanced disease who require prioritized treatment. HCV is now considered a curable disease due to advances in therapy, which have led to steadily increasing cure rates. Treating chronic HCV infection has a prevention benefit, as cured individuals can no longer transmit the virus. As of December 2013, six drugs were licensed for HCV treatment, including interferon-based therapies, ribavirin, protease inhibitors (boceprevir, simeprevir, telaprevir), and the nucleotide analog polymerase inhibitor sofosbuvir. However, treatment limitations include high costs, the need for specialized laboratory tests, and the toxicity of some medications. Genotyping the virus is essential before initiating treatment, as different genotypes require tailored regimens. The cost-effectiveness of HCV treatment programs is a significant consideration, given the high cost of medications and the need for regular monitoring and trained personnel. However, the benefits include improved patient outcomes and reduced transmission of the virus. Integrating HCV case-finding and treatment into specialist drug dependency services has also been shown to be cost-effective. WHO emphasizes the importance of human rights in HCV care, advocating for equitable access to testing and treatment and protecting individuals from discrimination and stigma. Quality care requires trained personnel, appropriate facilities, and access to necessary medications and laboratory services. Confidentiality and a non-coercive approach are fundamental principles in providing care for individuals with HCV infection.
